Question: Is it plausible that Ukraine is producing 100,000 FPV drones a month?
Answer: At the moment, they are producing far less than 100,000 FPV (first person view) drones per month. Unfortunately, as most of the FPV production facilities are rather small and in private hands, there’s no way to give an accurate number. 100k FPVs a months would certainly lower the demand for these valuable items on the frontline but I don’t see that this is the case right now. The good news is that Ukraine is ramping up its production and the 100,000 benchmark is a goal I expect them to attain very soon. One of the FPVs we’ve sent to the frontline earlier this year. However, even then, Ukraine will still need more FPVs. In a way, the FPVs are compensating for the lack of artillery shells on the frontline and play a more important role than they would do under more favorable circumstances. In addition, a lot of work has to be done to improve the ability of these weapons to withstand electronic warfare attacks against them. I’m optimistic that Ukraine will soon be able to produce FPVs in sufficient qualities and quantities. The good thing about it is that they don’t rely on other nations to pull this off, it all depends on their own capabilities. Question: Do soldiers really keep count of how many enemy troops they’ve killed?
Answer: Most often, you cannot be sure if the guy who dropped down after you shot at him is dead or just went for cover. Or maybe you hit him but he survived? In the chaos of battle, it’s also often impossible to say which of the hundreds of bullets that you and your buddies were shooting at the enemy soldier was the one that killed him. On the other hand, there are the “personal kills”. If you’ve emptied half of your magazine into the head of an enemy soldier standing five feet away, you certainly know. And you remember. Two Ukrainian members of a special purpose unit of the state security agency. We provided their rifle scopes. Some individuals In Ukraine have amassed spectacular kill counts that were impossible to achieve in prior conflicts. (Picture: private, all rights by the author) Many combat soldiers have a private “kill count” that is normally kept secret from everyone else (especially civilians). It usually goes like, “Well the guy on the edge of the trench on this day is a big maybe, and so are the two guys in the column we ambushed the other day, but the one who mistakenly ran into our trench? Well, he is dead and for sure, that was me!” So, yes, you keep count. Not with the same accuracy as an accountant in a bank but you do count the personal kills. Question: As a soldier, have you ever accidentally killed an innocent civilian?
Answer: Two peasants drove with their tractor over an anti-tank mine which I had placed there earlier. This happened in Kosovo during the time of the NATO airstrikes. There was a lot of fighting on the ground, especially in our area, but to my surprise, there were still some civilians around. We suspected that at least some of these folks were Serbian spies, but we couldn’t prove it. After an enemy offensive, my guerrilla unit had to withdraw to the mountains. Before we left, we mined all the approach routes the enemy could use. Whenever we encountered a farmer, we informed them about the mines so they could avoid getting hurt. Three days later, after the enemy offensive had ended, we returned to “our” valley” to remove the mines. Some of our devices had killed enemy soldiers, while others were duds, but when I arrived at a small road crossing where we had placed two anti-tank mines, I found an overturned and badly damaged tractor. In Kosovo, during the time of this incident. While looking for the second mine (the first one had been activated by the tractor), a peasant from a nearby village approached us and told us that two of his neighbors had been killed when their tractor drove over the mine. He pointed to a spot nearby where I could see a shoe covered in blood. We didn't tell him who had planted the mines. I didn't see any point in doing so. These people came from a village that (to my best knowledge) had never supported the guerrilla. And the fact that this guy had been around while our enemy was in the area made him double suspicious. I never thought twice about this incident, and I never felt bad about it. In war, sh*t happens.

Question: Does the Ukrainian government acknowledge that they will run out of troops before Russia does since Russia has a much larger population?
Answer: This issue is a bit more complicated. Ukraine acknowledges that is does not have enough troops (especially infantry); however, this is not because the recruiting pool has dried up. There are still between two and three and a half million able-bodied men inside Ukraine and another 600k in Western Europe. Ukraine could theoretically draft, train, and equip most of them but this would a.) cost a lot of money and b) completely ruin the economy. To get a recruit frontline ready costs about 20,000 dollars and this money has to come from somewhere. The main reason the Russians have fewer manpower problems than Ukraine is only partly due to their bigger population size: First of all, Russia doesn't care about the quality of the people they mobilize. Hard-core criminals, drug addicts, and mentally challenged people are always welcome to join. Of course, this makes for more recruits (without having to pull people away from their workplace and damaging the economy) but not for better ones. At the same time, the costs to train and mobilize these new “mobniks” are only a fraction of what Ukraine is paying. Again, lower costs mean you can recruit more people with less money. In addition, Russia often doesn't pay their soldiers’ salaries, doesn't take care of the wounded, and lets the dead ones rot on the battlefield (to avoid having to pay compensation to their families). Low quality: a destroyed Russian airborne tank. (Picture by the author of this post) The results of these two very different ways to mobilize more people for the military are seen on the battlefield: During the last two months, Russia has lost more than 1,000 soldiers every single day. Russian casualty rates are completely through the roof. At the same time, Ukraine’s casualty numbers remain low. There are no official statistics but they are under 200 troops per day. This is still too high, especially when you field quality soldiers and not cannon fodder, but because of an excellent medical system, the number is probably pretty close to a sustainable one. Furthermore, Ukraine’s casualty rates are low enough not to impact morale. Ukraine will be able to continue with its current recruiting approach for a long time. It's a careful balance between having enough money, keeping the economy going, maintaining morale, and sending enough people to the army. The Russians, on the other hand, will soon run out of expandable frontline material. Their prisons are already empty and their efforts to recruit ethnic minorities increasingly face resistance. The day the young men of Moscow and St. Petersburg will be called to the frontlines (i.e. the sons of the people who are profiting the most from Putin's war), this war will be over. These folks are only proud of their country & government as long as other people are doing the dying. When the recruiters come to knock on their doors, it will be the end of their adoration for Putin. Question: Are foot soldiers still the core of combat in the ongoing Ukraine and Russian war?
Answer: In Ukraine, the role of the infantry has changed a lot during the last months. Because of the constant drone threat, “classical” infantry tasks such as reconnaissance patrols on foot have become too dangerous. Instead, the military often uses reconnaissance drones. On the other hand, (mechanized) infantry still plays a major role in many combat operations. If you want to take ground from the enemy and hold it, you need foot soldiers. The “new” elite of the Armed Forces of Ukraine are the “Sturm” brigades, the assault units. These are highly qualified and well-equipped mechanized infantry troops that spearhead most attack operations. During a lecture to officers and officer candidates at a military academy. The war in Ukraine has already caused a lot of changes to the military training of many NATO countries. That performing many basic infantry tasks has become almost impossible, however, doesn’t mean that you don’t have to train this stuff anymore. In addition to the classical tasks, an infantry unit also needs to be qualified for drone operations (reconnaissance and strike drones) and electronic warfare (jamming the enemy’s drones). Mine clearance, especially during combat operations, is also something the infantry has to (re-)learn. During an attack, you simply don’t have the time to wait for the sappers to get rid of the mines in front of you. Due to the influence of foreign fighters, instructors, and advisors (not all of them Americans), many things have changed in the way the Ukrainians conduct war. Question: Do you think Ukraine made any tactical or strategic mistakes so far in the war against Russia?
Answer: When your country is invaded by a much stronger enemy, your strategic options are limited. You cannot expect the Ukrainians to execute any "genius" military operation that will turn the tide of the war. We must give a lot of credit to the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), not only for their heroic defense efforts but also for their attempts to regain the initiative on the battlefield. Outnumbered and lacking resources, the AFU nevertheless staged several large-scale operations, albeit with mixed results. While the counteroffensives in the Kharkiv region and Kherson in late 2022 were extremely successful, the "big" counteroffensive of last summer was a complete disaster. Now, around 30,000 Ukrainian troops have entered the territory of the Russian Federation in the Kursk region and they are seizing ground. This was a bold move for an army that lacks material and manpower. Unfortunately, this operation has weakened the eastern front line. Ukrainian forces in Donetsk have come under enormous pressure. This is an extremely dangerous situation, and I have the impression that the military and political leadership of the country has yet to grasp the seriousness of the Russian threats, especially in the Pokrovsk and Bakhmut directions. A damaged building in the city of Kupyansk, eastern Ukraine. (Picture by the author of this post) One of Germany’s most capable WWII strategists, the famous General Heinz Guderian, once said: “The Eastern front is like a house of cards. If the front is broken through at one point, all the rest will collapse.” This may very well happen in Ukraine. Despite this rather dire prognosis, I believe the Ukrainian Kursk operation was the right move. Ukraine brought the war to the Russians. However, Ukraine’s military leaders have overestimated the strengths and capabilities of their frontline units. Newly formed units that have never seen combat, staffed with inexperienced officers, will not have the same fighting power as a veteran brigade that has been in combat for more than two and a half years. In addition, defense preparations in many frontline areas have been neglected. This is due not only to wishful thinking (“We will liberate the occupied territories, so why do we need to prepare our cities for defense?”) but also to incompetence and even corruption. Ukraine has the best soldiers an army could wish for. They are motivated, brave, and tough. However, when it comes to the officer class, a different picture appears. Some of Ukraine’s highest-ranking generals are not much better than their Russian counterparts.

Question: Which assault rifle is best- the AK 47 or the M4 Carbine?
Answer: Some Ukrainian soldiers received an M4 (or a version of it) at the beginning of the war but later switched back to a Kalashnikov (an AKM with a 7.62x39mm caliber or an AK-74 with a 5.45×39mm cartridge). On paper, the M4s are the better weapons. They are lighter than most Kalashnikov versions, have integrated rails to easily attach an optic, and they’re also more accurate and compact. So why do some soldiers prefer the Russian AKs instead? I think it boils down to two reasons, personal preferences and your mission. For 95% of all combat jobs, the AKs are good enough. A Ukrainian soldier of a mountain infantry unit is carrying a AK version that has a rail system. For example, artillery soldiers of the Armed Forces of Ukraine will probably never shoot their weapons at an enemy and they also do not have to carry it around a lot. For them, the weight and accuracy of their rifles aren't that important. On the other hand, AK ammunition is easier to get in Ukraine and it’s also much cheaper. AK rounds lie around everywhere on the battlefield. Knowing that you’ll probably never run out of ammo for your rifle is a good feeling. The rail issue also has been solved. You can now buy very good Picatinny rails for Kalashnikov rifles that allow you to attach all kinds of stuff. A good rifle scope also solves the accuracy issue. Last but not least, many Ukrainian soldiers were trained on the AKs even before the Russian invasion. It was their first rifle and they are much more familiar with it than with any Western model. The Kalashnikov is also very balanced (you could call it ergonomic) which (in my opinion) is more important than carrying a bit of extra weight. The M4s and the AKs are both good rifles and you cannot say that one of them is “best”. In addition, there are so many variants of both rifle models around (nobody is using the original AK-47 anymore) that for every mission another version may turn out to be the best-suited one. After you’ve spent a week on the frontline, with all the shelling and shooting, you won’t even need a cot or a bed anymore: you’ll be so tired that you fall asleep immediately-while standing on your feet. A Ukrainian soldier at the frontline near Kupyansk. (Picture: Marian Kushnir) During a night march, I was supposed to be at the end of the column but fell asleep. When I woke up, I found myself somewhere in the middle. I had overtaken at least fifteen soldiers while I was in dreamland. I now observe the same dramatic effects of sleep deprivation in Ukraine. The frontline soldiers here can fall asleep whenever and wherever there’s even the smallest opportunity. No bed needed and no other comfort. And certainly not 120 seconds. Civilian drone operators do not need to be taught how to shoot a rifle or dig a trench. The reason the army is still using soldiers for these tasks is because it’s a dangerous job. Especially FPV pilots are working close to the frontline. It should be technically possible to pilot these drones from more remote places and people are already working on a solution to this problem. Therefore, I expect that civilians will soon (at least partially) take this role over from the army. In future wars, differences between military and civilian actors will become smaller.
